concepts.name: Types of Questions: Starred vs. Unstarred Questions
key_dimensions: Starred questions require oral answers and allow supplementary questions; unstarred questions require only written answers with no supplementaries allowed
Distinction in notice period requirements and order paper listing conventions
UPSC trap: Unstarred questions answered in written form are placed in Lok Sabha records but NOT read out — conceptual overlap with Zero Hour
Limit on number of starred (one per day per member) vs. unstarred questions (up to ten per day) a member can ask

concepts.name: Short Notice Questions: Conditions and Procedure
key_dimensions: Can be asked with shorter notice than prescribed minimum (10 days); Speaker/Chairman decides admissibility
Minister can decline to answer if not ready; urgency of the matter is the key criterion
Distinction from Starred questions: Short Notice questions are answered orally but are admitted on urgency grounds, bypassing normal notice periods
UPSC trap: Short Notice Questions are NOT the same as Zero Hour — they require prior notice, however short

concepts.name: Notice Period for Questions: Rules and Exceptions
key_dimensions: Minimum 15 days' notice required for Starred and Unstarred questions (Rules of Procedure, Lok Sabha)
Short Notice Questions are exceptions to the 15-day rule, subject to Speaker's discretion
Government's right to seek deferment vs. Speaker's power to admit despite short notice
UPSC trap: Notice period is prescribed by Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business, NOT by the Constitution

concepts.name: Private Members' Questions vs. Government Members' Questions
key_dimensions: Any member (including ruling party backbenchers) can ask questions — questions are NOT exclusive to Opposition
Ministers are questioned on subjects under their portfolios; private members can also be questioned on Bills introduced by them
UPSC trap: A question can be addressed to a private member relating to a Bill, Resolution, or matter connected with the business for which that member is responsible
Distinction from Private Members' Business: Question Hour is a different parliamentary device from Private Members' Bills/Resolutions

concepts.name: Supplementary Questions: Rules, Scope, and Limits
key_dimensions: Supplementary questions arise only from Starred questions — not permitted after Unstarred answers
Must arise directly from the original answer; cannot introduce new subject matter
Speaker's discretion in allowing or disallowing supplementaries; no fixed limit but time constraint applies
UPSC trap: Supplementary questions do NOT require advance notice — they are spontaneous, unlike the parent question

concepts.name: Questions to Private Members (Non-Ministers)
key_dimensions: A question can be addressed to a private member if the subject relates to a Bill, Resolution, or matter for which they are responsible
Rarely used provision but constitutionally and procedurally significant — a common MCQ trap
Governed by Lok Sabha Rule 40 — procedural basis often tested
Distinction: Most questions are to ministers; private member questions are the exception, not the rule

concepts.name: Admissibility Conditions for Questions
key_dimensions: Question must relate to a matter of public importance; must be within the responsibility of the Government of India
Cannot contain arguments, inferences, imputations, ironical expressions, or defamatory statements
Cannot anticipate a matter already on the agenda (Order Paper) or sub-judice matters
UPSC trap: Speaker is the sole authority on admissibility — no appeal lies from Speaker's decision on Question Hour

concepts.name: Question Hour Timing and Placement in Parliamentary Business
key_dimensions: Question Hour is the first hour of parliamentary sitting (11 AM–12 PM in Lok Sabha)
Can be suspended: during joint sittings, budget sessions on certain days, or by specific order of the House
UPSC trap: Question Hour is NOT constitutionally mandated — it derives from Rules of Procedure under Article 118
Distinction from Zero Hour which immediately follows Question Hour but has NO constitutional or rule-based status

concepts.name: Zero Hour: Constitutional Status, Origin, and Comparison with Question Hour
key_dimensions: Zero Hour starts at 12 noon; has NO mention in the Constitution or Rules of Procedure — purely a convention
Matters of urgent public importance are raised without prior notice — key distinction from Question Hour
Members raise issues on their own initiative; government is NOT obligated to respond unlike in Question Hour
UPSC trap: Zero Hour is an Indian parliamentary innovation with no parallel in British Parliament — frequently tested for its informal/non-statutory status

concepts.name: Suspension or Waiving of Question Hour
key_dimensions: Speaker/Chairman can suspend or curtail Question Hour in extraordinary circumstances (e.g., national emergency, disruptions)
Government can request deferment of specific questions; Speaker's consent required
COVID-19 precedent (2020): Question Hour was suspended during the Monsoon Session — a real-world application tested in current affairs
UPSC trap: Suspension of Question Hour does NOT require a constitutional amendment or a statutory provision — Rules of Procedure suffice

concepts.name: Half-Hour Discussion: Arising Out of Question Hour
key_dimensions: Used to raise a matter of sufficient public importance based on a question already answered during Question Hour or in writing
Held during last 30 minutes of the sitting on three days per week (Monday, Wednesday, Friday in Lok Sabha)
No formal motion or voting — purely deliberative device; minister may make a brief statement
UPSC trap: Half-Hour Discussion is NOT the same as Short Duration Discussion (Rule 193) — distinct procedural devices that are commonly confused

concepts.name: Role of Speaker/Chairman in Question Hour
key_dimensions: Speaker (Lok Sabha) / Chairman (Rajya Sabha) decides admissibility of questions — final authority
Can disallow questions that are repetitive, sub-judice, or relate to state list subjects not involving the Union
Can allow Short Notice Questions at their discretion; can also allow or disallow supplementaries
UPSC trap: Rajya Sabha Chairman has similar powers over Question Hour as Lok Sabha Speaker — but there are differences in specific rules between the two Houses

concepts.name: Questions on State List Subjects in Parliament
key_dimensions: Ordinarily, questions on State subjects cannot be asked in Parliament since ministers are not responsible for them
Exception: If a Central law covers a state list subject or if President's Rule is in force in a state
UPSC trap: During President's Rule, Parliament legislates for the state — questions on state administration become admissible
Constitutional basis: Article 356 and Schedule VII interaction creates this nuanced admissibility scenario

concepts.name: Sub-Judice Matters and Questions: Restrictions
key_dimensions: Questions on matters pending before courts (sub-judice) are generally not admissible to protect judicial independence
Speaker has discretion to allow a question if they feel it will not prejudice the judicial proceedings
UPSC trap: Sub-judice restriction is a Rule of Procedure limitation, NOT a constitutional prohibition — a conceptual distinction often tested
Comparison: Same sub-judice restriction applies to parliamentary debates under Article 105 but on different grounds

concepts.name: Questions in Rajya Sabha: Differences from Lok Sabha
key_dimensions: Both Houses have Question Hour; procedures are broadly similar but governed by separate Rules of Procedure
Notice period in Rajya Sabha is also 15 days for Starred/Unstarred questions; Short Notice questions also available
Key difference: Rajya Sabha being a continuing chamber does not have dissolution disruptions; questions lapse differently
UPSC trap: Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Vice President) is the presiding authority — NOT the Speaker — a basic but frequently confused fact

concepts.name: Lapsing of Questions: When a Lok Sabha is Dissolved
key_dimensions: All pending/admitted questions lapse upon dissolution of Lok Sabha — cannot be carried forward to new Lok Sabha
Rajya Sabha questions do NOT lapse on dissolution of Lok Sabha (Rajya Sabha is a permanent body)
UPSC trap: Questions lapse even if admitted and placed on the Order Paper but not reached during the session
Comparison with Bills: Bills also lapse on dissolution but with exceptions (e.g., Bills passed by Rajya Sabha) — parallel logic tested together

concepts.name: Oral Questions Ballot System and Listing
key_dimensions: When more Starred questions are received than can be orally answered, a ballot determines which questions are listed for oral answers
Only ~20 Starred questions are listed per day in Lok Sabha; rest are converted to Unstarred status and answered in writing
UPSC trap: A member submits a Starred question but it may be answered in written form if not reached — blurring Starred/Unstarred distinction in practice
The ballot system ensures fairness; governed by Lok Sabha Rule 33 — procedural specificity tested

concepts.name: Parliamentary Privilege and Question Hour: Immunity of Questions and Answers
key_dimensions: Members enjoy absolute privilege under Article 105(1) for anything said during Question Hour — cannot be sued for defamation
Ministers' answers in Question Hour also protected by parliamentary privilege
UPSC trap: Privilege protects speech but does NOT protect a member from action by the House itself (breach of privilege motion)
Deliberate misleading of the House through a Question Hour answer can attract breach of privilege — a nuanced area

concepts.name: Historical and Comparative Context: Question Hour in Westminster vs. Indian Parliament
key_dimensions: Borrowed from British Westminster tradition; UK Prime Minister's Questions (PMQs) — India has no equivalent PMQ session
Indian Question Hour is more structured with Starred/Unstarred classification; UK has different conventions
India's Zero Hour is a unique innovation not found in Westminster — demonstrates Indian parliamentary originality
UPSC trap: Indian Parliament follows Westminster model but with significant adaptations — examiners test on specific differences, not just similarities

concepts.name: Effectiveness of Question Hour as an Accountability Mechanism
key_dimensions: Question Hour is the primary tool for executive accountability to legislature on a daily basis
Declining effectiveness: Frequent disruptions and suspension of Question Hour reduce its accountability function
NITI Aayog / PRS Legislative Research data on hours lost and questions unanswered — governance dimension
UPSC Essay/GS2 angle: Reforms suggested — dedicated Question Time for PM (like UK), written question portals, strengthening committee scrutiny as complement
